title: Early intervention with repetitive theta burst stimulation in adolescents and young adults with depressive disorders: a sequential Bayesian, randomized controlled pilot trial
summary:
Depressive disorders are among the most common mental illnesses in late adolescence and early adulthood. They often have profound impacts on the social and professional lives of affected individuals and their relatives. In Germany, depression is treated according to medical guidelines with medications (antidepressants) and/or psychotherapy. However, especially in young people, medications often do not have the desired effect or are not tolerated by patients. Therefore, the development of further treatment options and their clinical evaluation is very important.

In this context, methods of so-called transcranial brain stimulation have been developed, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and Theta-Burst Stimulation (TBS), which represents an advanced form of TMS. TBS can increase the activity of certain areas of the brain transcranially (through the skull). This is achieved by holding a magnetic coil against the skull, which generates magnetic fields (based on the principle of electromagnetic induction) at the underlying spot, affecting the activity of nerve cells in that area. After stimulation, patients can continue their usual daily routines without restrictions. These procedures are considered safe, and the risk of side effects is low. The advantage of TBS over conventional TMS is primarily the significantly shorter daily treatment duration (a few minutes compared to about half an hour), which leads to less strain on patients.

The scientific background of the mentioned brain stimulation methods is that people with depression—unlike healthy individuals—often show altered activity in certain brain regions. There are indications that the activity of the left hemisphere in the anterior lateral area (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) is less pronounced compared to the right. TBS aims to influence the activity of nerve cells in these brain areas, thereby reducing depressive symptoms. To date, there are some indications of a favorable effect of these new methods on the severity of depression. A large American study in adults has shown that the effects of TMS and the newer TBS do not differ from each other. Moreover, there are initial smaller studies suggesting an effect of TBS also in young people with depression. However, the method has mainly been studied in people who have already had several unsuccessful attempts at medication therapy. In addition, previous studies often did not treat patients who, in addition to depression, have other psychological complaints such as anxiety disorders or difficulties in relationships.

In this study, we therefore want to investigate whether a 6-week treatment with TBS in young people with depressive disorders, who have not been treated with medication in the last 12 months (except for short-term on-demand medication), effectively reduces depressive symptoms. After completing the study treatment, we also want to examine the participants every 3 months for a total of 6 months to determine if the effects of the treatment persist beyond the treatment period.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Diagnosis of major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, or bipolar disorder with current depression (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, [DSM-5] criteria; assessed with the Diagnostic Interview for Mental Disorders [DIPS])
- No antidepressant or antipsychotic medication during the last 12 months, , except for short-term (< 2 weeks) on-demand medication
- Fluent in reading and speaking German
- Capable and willing to provide informed consent, as determined by the study
physician
Exclusion criteria:
- Positive screening for acute mania (defined by reaching the threshold “mild or greater” on at least one question from the Adult DSM-5 Self-Rated Level 1 Cross-Cutting Symptom Measure [from here on referred to as “APA screener”] Mania domain)
- Positive screening for acute psychosis (defined by reaching the threshold “slight or greater” on at least one question from the APA screener Psychosis domain)
- Comorbid Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), operationalized as meeting the
threshold of “mild or greater” on at least one item from the Repetitive Thoughts and
Behaviors domain of the APA screener, followed by clinical confirmation of OCD by
an experienced clinician
- Severe borderline typical psychopathology, defined as a very-high mean score on the self-reported Borderline Symptom List (BSL-23) of ≥2.671
- Primary substance use disorder except for nicotine and caffeine (DSM-5, assessed with the DIPS)
- Acute risk for suicidality, assessed by the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS; patient agrees to item 4 and/or item 5)
- History of brain surgery, significant and clinically relevant brain malformation or neoplasm, head injury, stroke, dementia or other neurodegenerative disorder 
- History of seizures
- Previous brain stimulation treatment (rTMS, transcranial direct current stimulation, electroconvulsive therapy, vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation)
- Cardiac pacemakers, intracranial implant, or metal in the cranium 
- Antiepileptic drugs and/or benzodiazepines corresponding to > 1mg lorazepam/day 
- Severe somatic comorbidity as judged by the study physician 
- Pregnancy (negative urine HCG test in women)
- Any clinically relevant findings in a structural MRI safety check (evaluated by a neuroradiologist)
- Investigators, site personnel directly affiliated with this study, and their immediate families (immediate family is defined as a spouse, parent, child or sibling, whether by birth or legal adoption)
